docs.title: KindTech
docs.text: Ergonomic Python access to UK public data. Geographic boundaries from the ONS ArcGIS Geoportal, statistics from the NOMIS API — with universal DataFrame support.

docs.title: Try it now — no install
docs.text:
Run a real notebook in your browser. Each one fetches live ONS data through the molab cloud runtime:

  • ONS statistics

    Browse and load datasets straight from the NOMIS API.

  • Geographic boundaries

    Explore LAD, LSOA and other UK boundary data interactively.

  • Boundaries + statistics

    Join geographic shapes with ONS data and map the result.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Install uk-open-data from PyPI:

uv add uk-open-data

KindTech depends on requests, narwhals, and python-calamine. You bring your own DataFrame library (pandas or polars). The package FAQ explains which subpackages are included and how they are released.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
from uk_open_data import load_geodata, load_ons, geodata_to_properties
import pandas as pd  # or polars

# Load LAD boundaries (GeoJSON) and extract properties
geojson = load_geodata(geography_type="LAD", year="2024")
geo_df = pd.DataFrame(geodata_to_properties(geojson, "LAD", 2024))

# Load ONS statistics — columns are normalised automatically
ons_df = load_ons("population", geography_type="LAD", time="latest")

# Join on the shared geography_code column
merged = geo_df.merge(ons_df, on="geography_code")

docs.title: Bring Your Own DataFrame
docs.text:
KindTech uses narwhals for universal DataFrame support. The library itself has no pandas or polars dependency — it returns whatever backend you have installed.

# With pandas installed → returns pd.DataFrame
from uk_open_data.ons import load_ons
df = load_ons("NM_1_1")
type(df)  # <class 'pandas.core.frame.DataFrame'>

# With polars installed → returns pl.DataFrame
from uk_open_data.ons import load_ons
df = load_ons("NM_1_1")
type(df)  # <class 'polars.dataframe.frame.DataFrame'>

If both are installed, polars is preferred (it's faster and more memory-efficient). The geo module returns plain GeoJSON dicts — no DataFrame backend needed.

docs.title: Why does this exist?
docs.text:
UK public data is powerful but painful to access programmatically. The ONS ArcGIS Geoportal has no developer documentation — just a point-and-click GUI. The REST API endpoint was discovered buried in the source code of an obscure UK government R package. NOMIS is slightly better documented but requires deep knowledge of SDMX query syntax and dataset codes that aren't surfaced anywhere obvious.

Every charity, social enterprise, and researcher working with UK geographic or statistical data ends up reverse-engineering the same APIs independently. KindTech wraps them so you don't have to — two function calls instead of hours of documentation archaeology.

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text: KindTech provides four modules for accessing UK public data, and analyses that put them to work on your own data:

docs.title: Geographic Data — uk_open_data.geo
docs.text:
Load UK geographic boundary data from the ONS ArcGIS Geoportal. Returns GeoJSON.

from uk_open_data.geo import load_geodata

# Load Local Authority Districts
boundaries = load_geodata(geography_type="LAD", coverage="UK")

docs.title: ONS Statistics — uk_open_data.ons
docs.text:
Load statistical data from the ONS NOMIS API. Returns pandas or polars DataFrames.

from uk_open_data.ons import load_ons

# Load Jobseeker's Allowance data
df = load_ons("NM_1_1", geography="TYPE480", time="latest")

docs.title: Postcodes — uk_open_data.postcodes
docs.text:
Resolve UK postcodes (and outcodes) to ONS geography codes via postcodes.io, so address data joins to boundaries and statistics. Returns pandas or polars DataFrames.

from uk_open_data.postcodes import postcodes_to_geography

# Postcodes -> LSOA, ready to join on `geography_code`
located = postcodes_to_geography(["SE13 7HX", "SE6 4RU"], geography_type="LSOA")

docs.title: Deprivation (IMD) — uk_open_data.imd
docs.text:
Load UK Indices of Multiple Deprivation, keyed on geography codes. A single nation returns its official index (England IoD 2025/2019 with all domains, or WIMD/SIMD/NIMDM); nation="UK" returns the mySociety composite for cross-nation comparison. Returns pandas or polars DataFrames.

from uk_open_data.imd import load_imd

imd = load_imd(nation="England")  # official IoD 2025; join on `geography_code`

docs.title: Analyses — uk_open_data.analyses
docs.text:
Ask a question of your own data. An analysis joins your table to open data and returns figures with their sources, the working, the choices made and the checks a person should do. Results hold totals only, never rows.

from uk_open_data.analyses import run_analysis

result = run_analysis(
    "reach-deprivation", clients, columns={"postcode": "Client postcode"}
)

docs.title: Design principles
docs.text:
• Flat functions — no classes to instantiate, just call load_geodata() or load_ons()
  • String or enum — pass "LAD" or GeographyType.LAD, both work
  • Bring your own DataFrame — narwhals returns whatever backend you have installed
  • Bundled catalogs — small CSV reference tables ship with the package (136KB total) so you can browse available datasets offline
  • Live data — actual geographic/statistical data is always fetched fresh from the source APIs
Copy Markdown

docs.title: Analyses
docs.text:
An analysis answers one question a charity asks of its own data. You give it a table, say which column is which, and it joins your data to UK open data and returns figures you can check and reuse.

Kindtech Evidence is built on these analyses. This page is about running them from Python. You can also run them from the command line, or from a chat assistant through the connector.

These analyses follow work first done by DataKind UK volunteers with charities. The case studies reproduce five of those projects.

Every analysis returns the same things:

  • an answer: one or two sentences that answer the question, and the three figures to show first
  • figures: the headline numbers
  • tables: totals behind the figures
  • a map description: which areas to draw and what to colour them by, when the analysis has a map
  • chart descriptions: which table and columns to draw as a bar chart
  • the working: each step taken, with how many rows went in and came out, the figures before rounding and the code that runs it again
  • choices: what the analysis decided for you, and the option that changes it
  • checks: what a person must confirm before using the figures
  • caveats: what the figures cannot say
  • sources: publisher, edition, licence and link for every dataset used
  • a privacy summary: what was hidden, and what left your machine

A result holds totals only. Nothing in it describes one person, and no value from your data is repeated back, not even in a warning or an error message.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
import pandas as pd
from uk_open_data.analyses import run_analysis

clients = pd.read_csv("clients.csv")

result = run_analysis(
    "reach-deprivation",
    clients,
    columns={"postcode": "Client postcode"},
)

result.answer                                   # the question, answered in a sentence
result.figure("share_most_deprived_20").value   # 41.3 (per cent)
result.table("by_decile").to_frame()            # pandas or polars DataFrame
[check.question for check in result.checks]     # what to confirm first
result.to_dict()                                # everything, as plain JSON types

data can be a pandas or polars DataFrame, or a list of row dictionaries. columns maps each role the analysis needs to one of your column names. You can leave a role out when your data already has a column with that name.

To run an analysis on a file without writing Python, use the command line.

docs.title: list_analyses()
docs.text:
Returns an AnalysisInfo for every analysis: its id, title, the question it answers, a summary, its roles (the columns it can use), its input_modes (the shapes of data it accepts), its options and its coverage.

Every option has two names. name is its code name, the one a call is written with, such as catchment. label is its short plain name, such as "Area you serve". Show the label beside the option. Every message that points a person at an option uses the label, in quotes ("Change 'Area you serve' to include them."), and never the code name, so the sentence matches what is on the screen. An option has the same label in every analysis that has it, and the result's choices use the same label for the choice it made:

name label catchment Area you serve catchment_min_share Share that makes a place part of your area suppress_below Smallest count shown postcode_lookup Where postcodes are looked up need People you are trying to reach top Places listed characteristic What people are grouped by groups How your labels match census groups under_represented_below What counts as under-represented within_km Distance within reach, in kilometres

The area an analysis looks across has one name wherever a person reads it: "the area you serve". catchment is only its code name.

A table's columns have plain names too. table.columns holds the ids, which a program reads, and table.headings maps each id to the heading to show, such as "Your people per 100 in need" for people_per_100_in_need. table.units gives the unit of each column that has one, named as the units of figures are: "percent" or "km". Show a table with its headings and units and it reads the same on a page, in a chat and on the command line. A place is a "Local authority" in most tables and a "Neighbourhood" in the one behind the first analysis's map.

An option that takes one of a fixed list of values lists them as choices, each with a value and a label a person can read, so a page can show a list to pick from. choices is empty when the option is free, such as a number or a place name. For the need option the choices are the built-in needs; a table of your own is still given as a mapping.

A role with reported set to True holds names the result uses too, such as local authorities, so the same names can appear in the result. Values of every other role are never repeated.

A reported role can also list reported_values. That is for a column that holds a person's own words as well, such as their ethnic group: only the listed values are names the result uses, and no other value in the column is ever repeated. If you check a result for values repeated from the input, leave out the listed values when there are any, compared without case, and check every other value in the column. Leave the whole column out only when the role is reported and lists no values.

A role with amount set to True holds a number the analysis adds up: a count of people or a volume. A total of it is in the result, so where one row is the only one for its place or group, that row's number comes back as the total. That is not a repeated value. A number in any other role, such as a latitude, never comes back.

docs.title: describe_analysis(analysis_id)
docs.text: Returns the AnalysisInfo for one analysis. Raises KeyError for an unknown id.

docs.title: run_analysis(analysis_id, data, columns=None, options=None)
docs.text:
Runs an analysis and returns an AnalysisResult.

Raises AnalysisInputError (a ValueError) when the data, the column mapping or an option cannot be used. The message is written for a person and error.problems lists each problem separately.

error.option is the code name of the option the error is about, and error.role the name of the column role, so a page can mark the right box and a program need not search the sentence. When the problems are about several, it is the first of them. Each is None when the error is about neither, for example when a source could not be read. The command line adds what to type: "On the command line this is --option catchment=VALUE."

When the columns an analysis needs were not all found, error.role is the first one still to be named. When an option was given that the analysis does not have, the message lists each option it does have by both names: "need ('People you are trying to reach')".

When a public data source the analysis needs cannot be reached, the requests.RequestException is let out. Its text holds the whole web address that was asked for, which can hold a postcode, so show a message of your own rather than the text. The command line names the site alone, and says whether the source could not be reached or answered with an error. An analysis needs no network when the public figures it uses are kept on your machine.

docs.title: record_run(analysis_id, input_mode, door)
docs.text:
Records that a run has given a person an answer, so that a host can count how often each analysis is used. It writes one record at INFO level to the uk_open_data.runs logger, and that is all it does: the package adds no handler and sends nothing anywhere. On a person's own machine nobody collects the records. A host that keeps its logs can count them.

from uk_open_data.analyses import record_run

record_run(result.analysis_id, result.input_mode, "page")
# run analysis=reach-deprivation mode=postcodes door=page

run_analysis never records a run by itself. Whatever gives the answer to a person calls record_run once, after the answer has been given: the command line does ("cli"), and a page ("page") or a chat assistant ("chat") built on these analyses should. A run that fails is not recorded.

The record holds the three words and nothing else. Each must be on a fixed list (a registered analysis, one of its input modes, one of the three doors), so no word from a person's data can reach a log. A word that is not on its list raises KeyError (the analysis) or ValueError (the mode or the door), and the message does not repeat it. The same three words are on the record as record.analysis_id, record.input_mode and record.door.

A host that keeps the records imports the logger's name, and the doors, from the package, so neither is typed out a second time:

import logging

from uk_open_data.analyses import DOORS, RUNS_LOGGER

logging.getLogger(RUNS_LOGGER).setLevel(logging.INFO)

docs.title: Drawing the map
docs.text:
A result describes its map; render_map draws it as an SVG picture with a key and the credits the data licences ask for.

from uk_open_data.analyses import render_map

svg = render_map(result)                  # the first layer: deprivation decile
svg = render_map(result, layer="people")  # people reached, in bands

with open("map.svg", "w", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
    handle.write(svg)

The picture is drawn from the result's own table of totals, so it shows nothing the result does not already hold. People are shown in bands, and the lowest band includes zero. Hover over an area in a browser to see its name and value. The colours adapt to a dark page.

A picture shows one layer, and its title says what the colour shows: "People reached, by neighbourhood". The first layer of a map is drawn in blue and the second in orange, so two pictures of one result do not look like the same measure. The shaded areas sit in a frame with a scale line. Up to twelve local authorities are named one by one; neighbourhoods are named by the local authority they are in. A name that would cover most of a small place is written beside it, where there is room, so its colour can be seen. Text is broken into lines to fit the width you ask for.

The places around the map are drawn in pale grey, with their names where a name fits, when you give their outlines. Only the part of each that the frame shows is written to the picture, so a large neighbour does not make the file large. Put them among the features of boundaries, or in a list under "surroundings". Codes listed under "focus" are the surrounding places that hold the shaded areas: each gets a darker line and its name. Codes listed under "shore" are surrounding places whose outline is where the land ends. The shaded areas are drawn no further than it, and the picture is framed on it. Use it when the outlines of the areas run out over water and the outline of the place that holds them does not.

boundaries = {
    "type": "FeatureCollection",
    "features": areas,           # outlines you already have
    "surroundings": nearby,
    "focus": ["E09000023"],
    "shore": ["E09000023"],
}
svg = render_map(result, boundaries=boundaries)

render_map fetches the outline of each area from the ONS Open Geography Portal. Only the public area codes of the area you serve, and of the local authorities near it, are sent. To draw without the network, pass boundaries= a GeoJSON FeatureCollection you already have; load_map_boundaries(result) fetches one you can save and reuse.

load_map_boundaries fetches the places around the map as well, and lists under "focus" the local authorities that hold a map's neighbourhoods. A map of up to 1,000 neighbourhoods or 20 local authorities is drawn large, so its outlines come from the full ones with detail finer than 10 or 20 metres left out. So do the local authorities that hold its neighbourhoods, and the other places a picture of the usual width shows when there are no more than 40 of them, so that neighbours meet. A place further off keeps its 200 metre outline.

The full outlines of local authorities stop at the shore. The only full outlines of neighbourhoods that are open run out to low water and to the middle of a river. So on a map of neighbourhoods the local authorities that hold them are also listed under "shore", and a river or a bay is left clear. When the fine outline of one of them does not come, nothing is listed and the neighbourhoods are drawn whole.

A map of more areas is drawn small and takes outlines simplified to 200 metres. Every map asks for every local authority at 200 metres, nearly three megabytes, to find the ones near it. That answer is kept in memory for the life of the process, so a second map does not ask again; uk_open_data.analyses.maps.clear_outline_cache() forgets it. When the places around cannot be fetched, the map is drawn without them and nothing is said.

The fine outlines usually come in a few seconds. At times the service has taken from a quarter of a minute to a minute or two for one map, and it is not known why. A program that cannot wait, such as one answering in a chat, calls load_map_boundaries(result, fine=False). It then gets the 200 metre outlines of every area, and the places around from the answer kept in memory, in a second or two. load_map_boundaries is safe to call from two threads at once.

docs.title: The answer
docs.text:
result.answer is one or two sentences that answer the question the analysis asks, for example:

Of your people in the area you serve, 49.0% live in the 20% most deprived neighbourhoods in England. Of everyone who lives in that area, 20.0% do, so you reach those neighbourhoods more than their share.

Open with it wherever you show a result, so a report, a page and a chat assistant all say the same thing. It is built from the figures and tables of the result, after small counts are hidden, so it says nothing the result does not already show. When the figure it rests on is hidden, it says so instead of giving a number. The places and groups it names are the public names in the result's tables, never text from your data.

The sentence is careful about what it calls a gap. A place is named as one to look at first only when it falls below the rate for the whole area, so a list of one or two places does not present the place you reach most as a gap, and a place whose count is hidden is not named. A count of every resident is called "residents", not "people in need". A group with nobody in your data is named last, with a line saying so, because it may be a group you do not record.

result.key_figures holds the ids of up to three figures to show first, in order. Each is a figure of the result, and none is hidden: when a figure that would be shown first is hidden to protect a small count, the next one takes its place.

for figure_id in result.key_figures:
    figure = result.figure(figure_id)
    print(figure.label, figure.value, figure.unit)

docs.title: Checking a result and running it again
docs.text:
A result shows its working, so that anyone can check it or run it again.

result.working lists each step in plain words, with how many rows went in and came out. result.sources gives each source and its date.

A share or a rate is rounded before it is shown. figure.exact is the value before rounding:

figure = result.figure("share_most_deprived_20")
figure.value   # 68.6
figure.exact   # 68.57142857142857

exact is None for a count, which is not rounded, and for a figure that is hidden to protect a small count. It is also None for a distance from one place to a site, which is rounded to the kilometre on purpose so that it says less about where a site is.

result.code is the Python that runs the analysis again with the same settings:

print(result.code)

# Version 0.1 of this analysis, run with
# uk-open-data 0.2.0. This runs it again with
# the same settings. No row or heading of your table is written
# here: put the name of your own column beside each role.
import pandas as pd

from uk_open_data.analyses import run_analysis

data = pd.read_csv("your-table.csv")
result = run_analysis(
    "reach-deprivation",
    data,
    columns={
        "postcode": "",  # the name of your column
    },
    options={
        "suppress_below": 10,
        "postcode_lookup": "auto",
        "catchment_min_share": 0.05,
    },
)
print(result.answer)
for figure in result.figures:
    print(figure.label, figure.value)

It prints the answer and every figure, to set beside the ones in the result.

Every setting that has a value is written out, the ones you left alone too, so the code gives the same result if a default changes in a later version. That is why it can hold a setting the list of choices in a result does not mention. A setting the analysis works out for itself, such as the area you serve when you named none, is left out. An area you named is written as you gave it.

The setting for where postcodes are looked up is written as it was used. Code copied from a run that kept postcodes on one machine says so, and on another machine it stops and asks for the postcode table before it sends a postcode anywhere.

The code holds no row and no heading of your table. The names of your columns are left for you to fill in, because a heading can hold something private. A setting that holds your own words, such as your own labels for groups in who-we-miss, is written as {} with a note to fill it in. So the code is as safe to share as the result is.

The command line prints both as the last two parts of its report, under "Figures before rounding" and "To run it again in Python". The code starts at the margin, so it runs as it is copied.

docs.title: Charts
docs.text:
result.charts describes the charts a result is best shown with, so a page can draw them without knowing the analysis. Each Chart names a table of the result, the column that names each group of bars (category_column) and one or more series, each a column with a label and a unit. Every series in a chart has the same unit, so one axis serves them all.

chart = result.charts[0]
frame = result.table(chart.table).to_frame()
frame.plot.bar(x=chart.category_column, y=[s.column for s in chart.series])

A value hidden to protect a small count is None in the table. Draw no bar for it.

docs.title: Small counts
docs.text:
A count from 1 to 4 that is about a named place or a group is returned as None, with suppressed set to True, and so is anything worked out from it. When hiding one cell would let it be worked out from a total, a second cell is hidden with it. So a hidden count is not always small: do not report a hidden cell as "fewer than 5". Every result says this in its privacy notes. Change the threshold with the suppress_below option; it cannot go below 3.

A result says which threshold was used in privacy.suppress_below. The analyses about sites, provision gap and access and distance, hide nothing, and for them it is None.

docs.title: Reach against deprivation
docs.text:
reach-deprivation answers: are we reaching people in the most deprived neighbourhoods? It covers England, using the English Indices of Deprivation 2025 on 2021 neighbourhoods (LSOAs).

It accepts two shapes of data:

Input mode Columns What it is postcodes postcode One row per person or case, with a home postcode neighbourhood_counts lsoa_code, count Already totalled by 2021 LSOA

In postcodes mode the analysis looks postcodes up in the postcode table on your machine when one is installed, and then no postcode is sent anywhere. Install it once with uk-open-data postcodes download. Without the table, the distinct, well-formed postcodes are sent to postcodes.io; no other column leaves your machine, and rows that are blank or not shaped like a postcode are never sent. The result says which happened, under choices and privacy. In neighbourhood_counts mode nothing leaves your machine.

The deprivation index is downloaded from gov.uk, or read from a copy kept on your machine when there is one. A result that used a copy says so in its sources and its working, with the note the copy was kept with.

The analysis then works out the area you serve: the local authorities that each hold at least 5% of the people it could place. The decile figures and the map are about the people who live there, so they can be set against everyone who lives there. People outside the area you serve are counted in the local authority table, and a warning says how many there are.

Figure Meaning people_supplied People in the data you gave people_located People placed in an English neighbourhood people_in_catchment People who live in the area you serve share_most_deprived_10 Share of them in the 10% most deprived neighbourhoods in England share_most_deprived_20 Share of them in the 20% most deprived neighbourhoods in England catchment_share_most_deprived_20 Share of residents of the area you serve who live in those neighbourhoods, for comparison reach_per_1000_most_deprived_20 People reached per 1,000 residents of those neighbourhoods reach_per_1000_elsewhere People reached per 1,000 residents in the rest of the area you serve

The chart people_by_decile sets the share of your people in each decile against the share of residents of the area you serve.

Table Rows by_decile One per deprivation decile: people, share of people, residents, share of residents, people per 1,000 by_local_authority One per local authority; authorities outside the area you serve with few people share one unnamed row by_neighbourhood One per neighbourhood in the area you serve: decile, residents, and people in bands. This feeds the map Option Default Meaning suppress_below 5 Counts above zero and below this are hidden postcode_lookup "auto" "offline" uses the table on your machine and fails without one, "online" uses postcodes.io, "auto" uses the table when it is installed catchment worked out A local authority name or code, a list of them, or "England" catchment_min_share 0.05 The share a local authority needs to join a worked-out area 
result = run_analysis(
    "reach-deprivation",
    clients,
    columns={"postcode": "Client postcode"},
    options={"catchment": ["Lewisham", "Greenwich"]},
)

Before you use the figures

Read result.checks and result.caveats. Deprivation is measured for neighbourhoods, not people: someone who lives in a deprived neighbourhood is not necessarily deprived.

docs.title: Need against reach
docs.text:
need-reach answers: where is need high and our presence low? It covers England and Wales, by local authority, and is the method of the Smart Works case study turned into a function.

It accepts two shapes of data:

Input mode Columns What it is postcodes postcode One row per person or case, with a home postcode area_counts local_authority, count Already totalled by local authority, named or coded

Postcodes are placed as in the first analysis: on your machine when the postcode table is installed, and with postcodes.io otherwise.

The analysis loads a count of people in need in every local authority from Nomis, divides the people you helped in each one by it, and lists the high-need local authorities where you reach the fewest people per 100 in need. A local authority is high need when its count is in the top quarter of the area you serve. With fewer than four places, the one with the largest count is high need.

Choose the need with the need option:

need People counted "unemployed" (default) Unemployed people aged 16 to 64, not counting full-time students, Census 2021 "unemployed_women" Unemployed women aged 16 to 64, not counting full-time students, Census 2021 "unemployed_men" Unemployed men aged 16 to 64, not counting full-time students, Census 2021 "residents" Everyone who lives there, of every age, Census 2021. Use it when what you offer is for anyone {"dataset": ..., "label": ..., "filters": {...}} Any table Nomis publishes by local authority. The filters are the category codes to add up. Counts are asked for (measures 20100) unless the filters name another measure

The three unemployment needs count the census group "Economically active (excluding full-time students): Unemployed", as the case study does. Full-time students who were looking for work are a separate census group and are not counted. To count them too, give the table form with both groups:

options = {
    "need": {
        "dataset": "NM_2124_1",
        "label": "Unemployed people aged 16 to 64, with full-time students",
        "filters": {
            "c2021_eastat_7": [2, 4],
            "c_sex": 0,
            "c2021_age_7": [2, 3, 4, 5],
        },
    }
}

The need figures are public. They are fetched from Nomis once for each need and then kept in memory for as long as the program runs; clear_need_cache() forgets them. To run with no request to Nomis at all, keep a copy on the machine, in the same data folder as the postcode table:

from uk_open_data.analyses.need_reach import download_need_figures, keep_need_figures

download_need_figures("unemployed")   # fetch once, when a server is built
download_need_figures("residents")    # so the map can shade need by its rate

# or keep figures of your own under a built-in need, for a demonstration
keep_need_figures(
    "unemployed",
    [("E09000023", "Lewisham", 9000), ("E09000011", "Greenwich", 8000)],
    note="invented for a demonstration.",
)

A result that used a kept copy says so in its sources and its working, with the note the copy was kept with.

The area you serve should hold the places you do not reach yet as well. Name it with catchment: a list of local authorities, or a country. When you leave it out, the analysis works the area out as the first analysis does: each local authority that holds at least 5% of the people located (catchment_min_share). When none does, every local authority in England and Wales is compared.

An area worked out this way holds only places you already reach, so it can show where your reach is low against need but not where you reach nobody. The result says so in a warning. To see the places you do not reach, name the area.

Figure Meaning people_supplied People in the data you gave people_located People placed in a local authority in England or Wales people_in_catchment People who live in the area you serve areas_compared Local authorities compared people_in_need People in need in the area you serve reach_per_100_in_need People you reached per 100 people in need, across the area high_need_areas Local authorities with high need high_need_areas_without_people High-need local authorities where you reached nobody share_of_people_in_high_need_areas Share of your people who live in high-need local authorities share_of_need_in_high_need_areas Share of people in need who live there, for comparison

The charts need_in_priority_areas and reach_in_priority_areas show people in need and people reached per 100 in need for the places in priority_areas.

The labels follow the need. When the need is every resident, the figures, the headings, the list, the working and the source say "residents" and "the local authorities with the most residents", not "people in need" and "high need". The fourth and fifth analyses do the same.

The answer says so when the area was worked out from your data: it opens "In the 7 local authorities where most of your people live". When a fifth or more of the people in your data could not be placed in the area you serve, it ends by saying how many are not counted. When some of them could not be placed in any local authority, which is a name or a postcode to put right, and others live outside the area, which is not a mistake, it says how many of each.

When only one local authority is compared every share is 100%, so key_figures names the rate and the two counts behind it instead: reach_per_100_in_need, people_in_catchment and people_in_need.

Table Rows priority_areas The high-need local authorities, your lowest reach first: people in need, people, people per 100 in need. It is a list in that order and no more: a place on it can have more reach than the area as a whole by_local_authority One per local authority compared, with need and reach in bands, and people in need for each 1,000 residents. This feeds the map

The map shades need by its rate, people in need for each 1,000 residents, in five equal groups. With fewer than five places, each is a group of its own, from the lowest group to the highest, and one place alone is in the middle group. The three groups of the reach layer work the same way. The note of a layer says so when its places are fewer than its groups, and says nothing of it otherwise. A count would make the largest places darkest whatever their need. The list of high-need places still goes by the count, as the case study does. The residents are the census count of everyone who lives in each local authority, loaded beside the need figures.

The map falls back to the count in two cases, and the result says which way it went in its choices (map_need) and in the note of the map's need layer. One is when the need is every resident, so there is no rate to work out. The other is when the need figures came from a copy kept on the machine and no copy of the residents is kept beside it: the analysis does not fetch them, so that a run kept off the network stays off it.

Option Default Meaning suppress_below 5 Counts above zero and below this are hidden postcode_lookup "auto" As for the first analysis need "unemployed" The need to compare your reach with catchment worked out A local authority name or code, a list of them, or "England", "Wales" or "England and Wales" catchment_min_share 0.05 The share a local authority needs to join a worked-out area top 10 How many places to list, from 1 to 50 
result = run_analysis(
    "need-reach",
    clients,
    columns={"postcode": "Client postcode"},
    options={"need": "unemployed_women"},
)

result.table("priority_areas").to_frame()

A local authority with a hidden count is still ranked. It is ranked as if it had the largest count that would be hidden, which depends on the threshold alone, so the order of the list gives nothing away.

Before you use the figures

Read result.checks and result.caveats. Low reach is not the same as unmet need: another organisation may already serve the place. Need is a count of people, so large local authorities are more likely to be listed.

docs.title: Who we are missing
docs.text:
who-we-miss answers: who do we reach less than their share of the people who live here? It covers England and Wales, and is the method of the Sobus case study turned into a function.

It accepts three shapes of data:

Input mode Columns What it is postcodes group, postcode One row per person, with their group and home postcode group_counts group, count Already totalled by group people group One row per person, with their group and no location

The group column holds each person's ethnic group, or their sex, in your own words. The analysis matches each label to a group the 2021 Census publishes, counts your people by group, and sets each group's share of your people against its share of the residents of the area you serve. A group is under-represented when its share of your people is below four fifths of its share of residents.

Choose what the column holds with the characteristic option:

characteristic Groups compared Census table "ethnic_group" (default) Asian, Black, Mixed, White, Other TS021 "sex" Female, Male TS008

Labels are matched by their wording. "Black Caribbean" is Black, "White and Black Caribbean" is Mixed, "Any other ethnic group" is Other, and "Not stated" matches nothing. People whose label matches nothing are counted, left out of the shares, and a warning says how many there are. Codes and short forms cannot be matched by wording, so say where they belong with the groups option:

result = run_analysis(
    "who-we-miss",
    clients,
    columns={"group": "Ethnicity", "postcode": "Client postcode"},
    options={"groups": {"BAF": "Black", "WBR": "White"}},
)

result.table("by_group").to_frame()

The result names the census groups. It never repeats one of your own labels. The group role lists the census group names as its reported_values, because a label of yours can be the same as one of them.

With postcodes the analysis works out the area you serve as the first analysis does: the local authorities that each hold at least 5% of the people it could place. People who live outside it are left out, because they are set against the residents of the area you serve. Without postcodes the analysis cannot tell where you work, so you must name the area with catchment.

The residents come from Nomis, for every local authority at once. They are public, are fetched once for each characteristic and are then kept in memory; clear_residents_cache() forgets them. To run with no request to Nomis, keep a copy on the machine, as for need figures:

from uk_open_data.analyses.who_we_miss import download_residents, keep_residents

download_residents("ethnic_group")   # fetch once, when a server is built

# or keep figures of your own, for a demonstration
keep_residents(
    "sex",
    [("E09000023", "Lewisham", {"Female": 156000, "Male": 144000})],
    note="invented for a demonstration.",
)
Figure Meaning people_supplied People in the data you gave people_in_catchment People set against residents: with postcodes, those who live in the area you serve people_matched People whose label matched a census group. The shares are of these people people_not_matched People with no label, or one that matched no census group residents Residents of the area you serve in the 2021 Census groups_under_represented Groups you reach less than their share of residents share_of_people_first_group Share of your people in the first of those groups share_of_residents_first_group Share of residents in that group

The last two are the two shares the answer quotes, each with its value before rounding. They are there when the answer quotes them: when a group is reached less than its share and has people in your data.

The chart people_against_residents sets the share of your people in each group against the share of residents.

Table Rows by_group One per census group: people, share of people, residents, share of residents, representation (the first share divided by the second) and whether the group is under-represented Option Default Meaning suppress_below 5 Counts above zero and below this are hidden postcode_lookup "auto" As for the first analysis characteristic "ethnic_group" What the group column holds groups none Your label to census group, for labels the wording does not settle catchment worked out from postcodes A local authority name or code, a list of them, or "England", "Wales" or "England and Wales". Needed when there are no postcodes catchment_min_share 0.05 The share a local authority needs to join a worked-out area under_represented_below 0.8 A group is under-represented below this fraction of its share of residents

A group with a hidden count is not judged. A group nobody came from has a count of zero, which is shown, and is under-represented.

This analysis has no map yet. The residents are compared across the whole area you serve, not place by place.

Before you use the figures

Read result.checks and result.caveats. A gap is not proof of a barrier: groups differ in age and in need, and the census counts residents of every age. With few people, a gap can be chance. Do not publish two runs with different areas side by side, because a small count can be worked out by taking one from the other.

docs.title: Provision gap
docs.text:
provision-gap answers: where is provision thin against need across a region? It covers England and Wales, by local authority, and follows the method of the Starlight case study: total what is provided in each place, divide by the people it is for, and look at the places where need is high and provision is thin.

The analysis is about sites and what they provide, not about people. It accepts three shapes of data:

Input mode Columns What it is sites postcode, volume One row per site or service, with how much it provides area_volumes local_authority, volume Already totalled by local authority, named or coded site_list postcode One row per site or service. Each site counts as one

The volume is a number of zero or more: sessions, places, boxes, hours. A row whose volume is not a number stops the run, and the message says how many rows to correct. Postcodes are placed as in the first analysis: on your machine when the postcode table is installed, and with postcodes.io otherwise.

The analysis loads a count of people in every local authority from Nomis, divides the provision in each one by it, and lists the high-need local authorities with the least provision per 1,000 people. A local authority is high need when its count is in the top quarter of the area you serve, as in the second analysis.

The need option takes the same values as in the second analysis, and the same kept copies (keep_need_figures, download_need_figures) are used. The default here is "residents", everyone who lives in the place, because provision is often for anyone. Choose a narrower need when what you provide is for a group Nomis counts.

Figure Meaning volume_supplied Provision in the data you gave volume_located Provision placed in a local authority in England or Wales volume_in_catchment Provision in the area you serve areas_compared Local authorities compared areas_without_provision Local authorities where you provide nothing people_in_need People in need in the area you serve volume_per_1000_in_need Provision per 1,000 people in need, across the area high_need_areas Local authorities with high need high_need_areas_without_provision High-need local authorities where you provide nothing share_of_provision_in_high_need_areas Share of your provision that is in high-need local authorities share_of_need_in_high_need_areas Share of people in need who live there, for comparison

The charts need_in_priority_areas and provision_in_priority_areas show people in need and provision per 1,000 in need for the places in priority_areas. The map has two layers, need and provision.

Table Rows priority_areas The high-need local authorities, thinnest provision first: people in need, volume, volume per 1,000 in need. The labels follow the need, as in the second analysis by_local_authority One per local authority compared, with need and provision in bands. This feeds the map Option Default Meaning postcode_lookup "auto" As for the first analysis need "residents" The people to set your provision against catchment England and Wales A local authority name or code, a list of them, or "England", "Wales" or "England and Wales" top 10 How many places to list, from 1 to 50 
result = run_analysis(
    "provision-gap",
    sites,
    columns={"postcode": "Site postcode", "volume": "Sessions a year"},
    options={"catchment": "Wales"},
)

result.table("priority_areas").to_frame()

This analysis hides no count, and has no suppress_below option. Provision is what an organisation provides, not a number of people, so every total is shown, however small. Where a local authority holds one site, the provision shown for it is that site's. If your numbers are people, such as people seen at each site, use the need against reach analysis instead, which hides small counts. The result still names no site and repeats no postcode.

The case study compares England's Integrated Care Boards and uses hospital admissions as the need. This analysis compares local authorities and takes the need from Nomis. Health boards, and a need column of your own, are not in it yet.

Before you use the figures

Read result.checks and result.caveats. Thin provision is not the same as unmet need: another organisation may already provide there. Provision is counted where a site is, and people travel. Need is a count of people, so large local authorities are more likely to be listed.

docs.title: Access and distance
docs.text:
access-distance answers: how far are people from our nearest site, and where would a new site help most? It covers England and Wales, by local authority, and follows the method of the Material Focus case study.

Like the provision gap analysis, it is about sites, not about people. It accepts two shapes of data:

Input mode Columns What it is site_coordinates latitude, longitude One row per site, in degrees. West is negative site_postcodes postcode One row per site. Placed on your machine when the postcode table and the centres of neighbourhoods are there

A row whose position is outside the United Kingdom is left out and counted; that is also what happens when the two columns are swapped. A site in Scotland or Northern Ireland still counts as a site.

docs.title: Site postcodes that stay on your machine
docs.text:
The postcode table holds the neighbourhood of each postcode but no position. So the analysis places a site at the centre of its neighbourhood, from a file of neighbourhood centres kept on your machine. In a town that moves a site by a few hundred metres, and in the countryside by up to a few kilometres; the result carries a caveat that says so. Keep the centres once, when a server is built:

from uk_open_data.analyses.access_distance import download_centres

download_centres("neighbourhood")   # about 35,700 centres, about 1 MB

What happens to site postcodes follows postcode_lookup:

postcode_lookup Postcode table installed No postcode table "auto" (the default) Placed on your machine. Nothing is sent Sent to postcodes.io "offline" Placed on your machine. Nothing is sent The analysis stops "online" Sent to postcodes.io Sent to postcodes.io

With a postcode table installed and no centres kept, the analysis stops and names the function to run. It never falls back to sending postcodes, and it never fetches the centres while an analysis runs. A server that sets "offline" cannot send a postcode. The result says which happened, under choices and privacy.sent_to_third_parties.

The table and the centres cover England and Wales. On your machine, a site with a Scottish or Northern Irish postcode is not found and is left out and counted; give its latitude and longitude instead.

The analysis loads the people in every local authority from Nomis and the centre of every local authority from the ONS Open Geography Portal. For each local authority it measures the distance in a straight line from the centre to your nearest site, to the nearest kilometre. A local authority is within reach when that distance is within_km or less. The list shows the local authorities beyond reach, with the most people first: the places where a new site would bring the most people within reach.

Distance is not travel time. The package has no road or public transport times, so the analysis does not turn kilometres into minutes. And it measures from the centre of a local authority, not from where each person lives, which is rough for a large rural one.

The need option takes the same values as in the second analysis, and the same kept copies. The default is "residents". The centres can be kept on the machine too, so the analysis runs with no request at all:

from uk_open_data.analyses.access_distance import download_centres, keep_centres

download_centres()   # fetch once, when a server is built

# or keep centres of your own, for a demonstration
keep_centres(
    [("E09000023", 51.45, -0.02), ("E09000011", 51.47, 0.05)],
    note="invented for a demonstration.",
)

# the same for the centres of neighbourhoods, which place site postcodes
keep_centres(
    [("E01003189", 51.46, -0.01)],
    note="invented for a demonstration.",
    level="neighbourhood",
)
Figure Meaning sites_supplied Sites in the data you gave sites_located Sites placed in the United Kingdom areas_compared Local authorities compared people_in_need People in the area you serve average_distance_km Average distance from the centre of each person's local authority to your nearest site. A place with many people counts for more share_of_people_within_reach Share of people in a local authority whose centre is within within_km of a site people_beyond_reach People in a local authority whose centre is farther than that areas_beyond_reach Local authorities whose centre is farther than that farthest_distance_km Distance from the centre of the farthest local authority to a site

Every distance is from the centre of a local authority, the one the ONS publishes for it, and every person is counted there. That is coarse. A London borough is a few kilometres across, so 10 km says something about it. A large rural local authority can be 50 km across: a site can be inside it and still be farther than 10 km from its centre, and the place is then listed as far from a site. The answer, the labels, the headings and a caveat all say that distance is from the centre. Where the places you work in are large, set within_km higher and read the distances, not only who is within reach.

The charts people_in_priority_areas and distance_in_priority_areas show the people and the distance for the places in priority_areas. The map has two layers, distance and need.

Table Rows priority_areas The local authorities beyond reach, most people first: people, distance in kilometres. Empty when every place is within reach by_local_authority One per local authority compared, with people and distance in bands. This feeds the map Option Default Meaning postcode_lookup "auto" How site postcodes are placed. See the table above need "residents" The people to measure distance for catchment England and Wales A local authority name or code, a list of them, or "England", "Wales" or "England and Wales" within_km 10 How many kilometres from a site counts as within reach top 10 How many places to list, from 1 to 50 
result = run_analysis(
    "access-distance",
    sites,
    columns={"latitude": "Lat", "longitude": "Long"},
    options={"catchment": "Wales", "within_km": 15},
)

result.table("priority_areas").to_frame()

This analysis hides no count, and has no suppress_below option. The result names no site and repeats no postcode or position. Distances are rounded to the kilometre, but the distances from several local authorities can still show roughly where a site is.

Confidential addresses

Do not share a result if the address of a site is confidential, such as a refuge. A check in every result asks this.

Before you use the figures

Read result.checks and result.caveats. The figures say how far people are from a site. They do not say how far the people you see travel, or whether anyone far away needs you.

docs.title: Writing an analysis
docs.text:
An analysis is an AnalysisInfo and a function that takes an AnalysisInput and returns an AnalysisResult. Register it with register_analysis. The rules every analysis keeps:

  1. Totals, never rows. Report problems by how many rows they affect.
  2. Hide small counts and anything that gives them away. Do not publish two breakdowns that can be taken from each other to get a small count. Say in the privacy notes that a hidden count is not always small.
  3. Give every figure a source.
  4. State every choice and name the option that changes it. Give each option a label, use the label in quotes whenever a sentence points at the option, and pass option= or role= when you raise AnalysisInputError. Give a table headings for any column the package has no heading for.
  5. Leave checks for a person to answer.
  6. List anything sent off the machine in privacy.sent_to_third_parties.
  7. Answer the question in answer, from figures the result shows and nothing else, and name the figures to show first in key_figures.
  8. Give a share or a rate its exact value, from before_rounding, when the figure is shown, and never when it is hidden. Mark an option private when the value a person gives holds words from their own data, so the code that runs the analysis again leaves it out. run_analysis writes result.code for you.
Copy Markdown

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
The package installs one command under two names, uk-open-data and kindtech. It runs analyses on a file without writing any Python.

uv add uk-open-data pandas        # the command needs pandas or polars installed
uv run uk-open-data analysis list

docs.title: analysis list
docs.text:
Lists every analysis with the question it answers. Add --json for the full descriptions.

uk-open-data analysis list
# reach-deprivation: Are we reaching people in the most deprived neighbourhoods?

docs.title: analysis describe ANALYSIS_ID
docs.text:
Shows what an analysis needs: the shapes of data it accepts, the columns, and the options with their defaults. Add --json for the same as JSON.

uk-open-data analysis describe reach-deprivation

docs.title: analysis run ANALYSIS_ID FILE
docs.text:
Runs an analysis on a .csv, .xlsx or .ods file and prints a plain-text report: a sentence or two that answer the question, then the figures, the tables, the checks to make before using them, what the figures cannot say, the choices made, the working, the figures before rounding, the sources, a privacy summary and the Python that runs it again. A number has its unit after it, such as "64.7 km", unless the label beside it already says the unit.

uk-open-data analysis run reach-deprivation clients.csv \
    --column postcode="Client postcode"
Flag Meaning --column ROLE=COLUMN Which of your columns plays a role. Repeat it for each role --option NAME=VALUE Change an option. Repeat it for each option --sheet NAME The sheet to read from a spreadsheet. The first sheet is read by default --json Print the whole result as JSON instead of a report --summary With --json, leave out the rows of long tables such as map data --output PATH Write to a file instead of the screen --map PATH Also draw the map and save it as an .svg file --map-layer LAYER What the map is coloured by, for example people. The first layer is used by default

An option value is read as JSON when it is JSON, and as text otherwise:

uk-open-data analysis run reach-deprivation clients.csv \
    --column postcode="Client postcode" \
    --option suppress_below=10 \
    --option catchment='["Lewisham", "Greenwich"]'

When the file, a column or an option cannot be used, the command prints what is wrong and exits with status 2. The message never repeats a value from your data, so it is safe to paste into a chat or an issue.

A message names an option by its plain name, as a page shows it, such as 'Area you serve'. When an error is about one option or one column, a last line says what to type here: "On the command line this is --option catchment=VALUE." analysis describe lists every option with both names.

The outlines for --map come from the ONS Open Geography Portal. They usually come in a few seconds, but at times the service takes a minute or two to answer, so the command first writes "Fetching the outlines for the map ..." to standard error. The report on standard output is not changed by it. When the outlines cannot be fetched, the report is still printed or written, no map file is made, and the command says so in one sentence and exits with status 3. Status 3 means the report is whole and only the map is missing, so a script can keep the report. Status 2 means nothing was made.

A run that prints its answer writes one line to the uk_open_data.runs logger, with the analysis, the input mode and the word cli. Nothing collects it on your machine and nothing is sent anywhere. See record_run.

docs.title: postcodes download
docs.text:
Fetches the postcode table, a few megabytes, so that analyses look postcodes up on your machine and send none of them out. Run it once. --force fetches it again, and --url with --sha256 fetches a copy you host yourself.

uk-open-data postcodes download

docs.title: postcodes info
docs.text: Shows the installed table's edition, size and the credits to show when you publish something made with it. With no table installed it says so, says first that an analysis still works, by looking postcodes up with postcodes.io and saying so in its result, and then says how to get a table. That is not an error.

docs.title: postcodes build SOURCE TABLE --edition EDITION
docs.text: Builds a table from the ONS best-fit postcode lookup (.csv, or the .zip it comes in) and prints its SHA-256. This is how a new edition is published; you do not need it to use the package.

docs.title: connector
docs.text:
Starts the connector, which offers the analyses to a chat assistant as tools. It is the same as python -m uk_open_data.connector and takes the same options:

uk-open-data connector
uk-open-data connector --transport streamable-http --port 8000

It needs the connector extra, and says so when the extra is not installed:

uv add "uk-open-data[connector]"

Over stdio, the default, the command prints nothing and waits: the assistant starts it and talks to it. It runs until the assistant, or you, stop it.

docs.title: Using it from an assistant
docs.text:
Give an assistant the JSON summary, not your file:

uk-open-data analysis run reach-deprivation clients.csv \
    --column postcode="Client postcode" --json --summary

The summary holds totals only, with small counts hidden. Your rows stay on your machine.

Copy Markdown

docs.title: Connector for chat assistants
docs.text:
The uk_open_data.connector module offers the analyses and open data to a chat assistant, such as Claude or ChatGPT, over the Model Context Protocol. A charity worker asks a question in their own words; the assistant calls a tool; figures come back with their sources.

Every tool is read-only, and every tool keeps one rule: the assistant sees totals, never rows.

docs.title: Start it
docs.text:
The server needs the connector extra:

uv add "uk-open-data[connector]"
uv run uk-open-data connector

With pip it is pip install "uk-open-data[connector]", then uk-open-data connector. Started without the extra, the command ends with one sentence that says how to install it.

python -m uk_open_data.connector starts the same thing and takes the same options. That runs over stdio, which is how a desktop assistant starts a local connector. For Claude Desktop or Claude Code, add this to the MCP configuration, with the path to your checkout:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "kindtech": {
      "command": "uv",
      "args": [
        "run", "--directory", "/path/to/uk-open-data", "--extra", "connector",
        "uk-open-data", "connector"
      ]
    }
  }
}

To host it, run the same server over Streamable HTTP. The address to give an assistant then ends in /mcp:

uv run uk-open-data connector --transport streamable-http --port 8000

docs.title: Tools
docs.text: Tool What it does find_analysis Finds the analysis that answers a question, and says what data it needs. describe_place Describes a place in England from the Indices of Deprivation 2025. run_analysis_on_counts Runs an analysis on counts that are already totalled by area or by group.

docs.title: find_analysis
docs.text:
query is the question in the person's words, or left out to list every analysis. The answer holds each analysis description, best match first.

An analysis that takes no totals cannot run in a chat. needs_rows in the answer names the listed analyses of that kind and says where they can run. The access and distance analysis is one: it needs a row per site that says where the site is.

docs.title: describe_place
docs.text:
place is a local authority name or code, a 2021 LSOA code or a postcode district such as SE13.

from uk_open_data.connector import describe_place

answer = describe_place("Lewisham")
answer["status"]            # "found"
answer["place"]["code"]     # "E09000023"
answer["figures"]           # neighbourhoods, residents, shares in the most deprived areas
answer["tables"]            # by deprivation decile, and by type of deprivation
answer["sources"]           # publisher, edition, licence and link

status is found, choose (several places match, listed in matches), not_found, not_covered (outside England), not_accepted (a full postcode or a street address) or unavailable (a data source could not be reached).

A full postcode is not accepted, even a venue's, because nothing tells a venue's postcode from a person's home. It is not looked up, sent anywhere or repeated, and the message asks for the first half of the postcode or the name of the place. For one neighbourhood, pass its 2021 LSOA code.

A street address is not accepted either: a postcode inside other words, or a number beside a word such as "Road", "Flat" or "House". The tool describes areas, not buildings, and an address can be a person's home. The message says an address should not be sent and asks for the council area or the first half of the postcode.

The tool describes places in England only, because the deprivation index it reads is England's. A council, code or postcode in Wales gives not_covered with a message that says the place is in Wales and that the analyses which cover England and Wales still work for it.

The deprivation index is read from a copy kept on this machine when there is one, and the source in the answer then says so. When you host the connector, keep it when the image is built (uk_open_data.imd.download_imd), so the first call does not wait on a download. A copy kept with uk_open_data.imd.keep_imd that leaves out the types of deprivation gives the same answer without that table, and says so in warnings. A copy that cannot be read gives the status unavailable.

A postcode district is looked up in the postcode table on this machine when one is installed, so it is not sent anywhere. Without a table it is sent to postcodes.io. Either way the answer says which happened under privacy. When you host the connector, install the table when the image is built (uk-open-data postcodes download), so a district stays on your server.

docs.title: run_analysis_on_counts
docs.text:
analysis_id names the analysis. counts holds one object per area or group, keyed by the role names of an input mode the analysis marks as aggregated. options changes the analysis options.

Analysis One row of counts Options it needs reach-deprivation {"lsoa_code": "E01003189", "count": 12} none need-reach {"local_authority": "Lewisham", "count": 120} none who-we-miss {"group": "Black Caribbean", "count": 40} catchment, the area you serve provision-gap {"local_authority": "Lewisham", "volume": 1200} none

A volume is what the charity provides in that place, such as sessions, places or hours. The provision gap analysis hides no small figure, because a volume is not a count of people, and its result says so.

The answer holds the analysis result without the rows of its detail tables, so an assistant is not handed a row per neighbourhood. Such a table comes back with its columns and no rows, and rows_left_out in the answer names those tables and says they are not empty, so that an assistant does not report "nothing found". Where the result's map is drawn from one of them, the note says the map cannot be drawn from the answer. Rows about individual people, such as one postcode per person, are refused, and so is one row per site.

The result holds answer, one or two sentences that answer the analysis's question, and key_figures, the ids of the figures behind them. Both come through as the analysis wrote them. Where a result has an answer, open_with tells the assistant to begin its reply with that sentence in its exact words, so a person reads the same words in a chat as on the Kindtech Evidence page and at the command line. The sentence passes the same check as the rest of the result: it is withheld if it repeats a value from the rows.

The result also holds what a person needs to check it. A share or a rate has exact, its value before rounding, and the result has code, the Python that runs the analysis again with the same settings. Both are described under the working and come through as the analysis wrote them. The code leaves the names of the person's columns to be filled in, and a setting that holds their own labels, such as groups for who-we-miss, is written as {}, so it passes the same check as the rest of the result. The server's instructions and the tool's description tell an assistant to quote figures as they are shown, rounded, and to give an exact value or the code only when the person asks how a figure was worked out or asks for the code.

A count or volume given as text that is nothing but a number, such as "1200" or "1,200", is read as a number, because assistants often send one that way. This applies to the roles an analysis marks amount in its description and to no other. Any other text there is left for the analysis, which says how many rows to correct.

from uk_open_data.connector import run_analysis_on_counts

answer = run_analysis_on_counts(
    "need-reach",
    [
        {"local_authority": "Lewisham", "count": 120},
        {"local_authority": "Greenwich", "count": 40},
    ],
    options={"catchment": ["Lewisham", "Greenwich", "Bexley", "Bromley"]},
)
answer["status"]              # "ok"
answer["result"]["answer"]    # the sentence to open with
answer["result"]["figures"]   # headline figures, small counts hidden
answer["result"]["tables"]    # the high-need places, lowest reach first

catchment is the area you serve: every place the charity serves, whether or not it reaches anyone there yet. Without it, need against reach compares only the local authorities that hold at least 5% of the people in the rows, so it cannot show a place the charity does not reach yet, and its result says so in a warning. With one place there is nothing to compare, and the answer says that too. An assistant should ask the person for the area they serve when the question is about where they are missing.

status is ok, would_hide_counts, input_problem (problems lists what to fix, for example an option the analysis needs), needs_rows, unknown_analysis or unavailable (a data source the analysis needs could not be reached).

A problem sentence is written for the person and names an option by the label they read, in quotes: "Change 'Area you serve' to include them." An assistant passes options by their code names, so when the analysis says which one a problem is about, the answer also has option (for example catchment) or role (the column, for example count). find_analysis lists each option's label beside its name.

needs_rows is the answer for an analysis that takes no totals, such as the access and distance analysis, whatever rows are passed. Its message says the analysis cannot run in a chat, because it needs a row for each site and this tool takes totals only, and that it runs on the Kindtech Evidence page or with the command line tool.

docs.title: The map
docs.text:
An analysis result describes a map, and the table that feeds it is one of the tables left out of an answer. So the server draws the map itself, one picture for each thing the map can be coloured by, and sends the pictures beside the answer: in the tool result's _meta, under kindtech/map, which is for the app the person is using and is not part of what a model is given. The tool points to a small page, ui://kindtech/analysis-map.html, that shows them. An assistant app that supports MCP Apps shows that page with the answer, so the person sees the map in the chat. An app that does not shows the answer alone, as before.

The answer itself gains map, with drawn and a note for the assistant: a picture was drawn for the person and the assistant is not given it, or why none was drawn. An analysis with no map has no map in its answer, and neither has a result that was held back. The plain Python function run_analysis_on_counts draws nothing; only the server does.

The outlines are fetched from the ONS Open Geography Portal each time a map is drawn. What is sent is public area codes only: those of the areas on the map and of the local authorities near it, which are drawn pale around it. When the outlines cannot be fetched the figures come back as usual and the note says no map was drawn.

The figures do not wait long for a picture. A map in a chat is drawn from the quick outlines, simplified to 200 metres, where the page and the command line ask for finer ones. Outlines usually come in a few seconds, but at times the boundary service has taken a minute or more for one map, and it is not known why. So the server waits 15 seconds for the outlines and then sends the answer without a map, with a note that says so and suggests running the analysis again in a few minutes. The fetch is left to finish. The outlines of every local authority are kept in memory once fetched, for as long as the server runs.

When you host the connector, keep the outlines on your server and pass a function that reads them, so that no run waits on another service:

from uk_open_data.connector import build_server

server = build_server(map_boundaries=outlines_kept_here)  # takes an analysis result

Pictures of more than about 1.5 MB together are not sent: the first layers that fit are, and when not even one fits the note says so.

docs.title: When counts would be hidden
docs.text:
An analysis hides a count from 1 to 4, and where it hides one count in a table it hides a second, so the first cannot be worked out from the total. In a chat that second count can be a number the person has just typed, which reads as a fault. So when the answer would hide any figure or table row, the first call holds it back and says so:

answer = run_analysis_on_counts(
    "reach-deprivation",
    [
        {"lsoa_code": "E01003189", "count": 3},
        {"lsoa_code": "E01003190", "count": 30},
    ],
)
answer["status"]       # "would_hide_counts"
answer["would_hide"]   # {"figures_and_rows": 3, "counts_below": 5}
answer["choices"]      # combine the small counts first, or run as it is

The answer holds no figure from the run and nothing from the rows. The person then chooses. They can add each small count to a neighbouring area's count, or to a broader group's, and send the rows again, saying with the figures which rows were combined. Or they can take the result with those counts hidden:

answer = run_analysis_on_counts(analysis_id, counts, hidden_counts="accept")
answer["status"]       # "ok"

An analysis that hides nothing, such as the provision gap analysis, never asks.

When you host the connector, keep the public figures three of the analyses compare with on the server when the image is built, so a run does not wait on Nomis: uk_open_data.analyses.need_reach.download_need_figures for the need against reach analysis, the same function called with "residents" for the provision gap analysis, which sets provision against everyone who lives in a place unless told otherwise, and uk_open_data.analyses.who_we_miss.download_residents for the who we are missing analysis.

The "residents" figures serve two analyses. Need against reach uses them too, to shade its map by people in need for each 1,000 residents. When the need figures are kept and the residents are not, it does not fetch them: the map is shaded by the count and the result says so in its choices. Keep both and the map goes by the rate.

docs.title: The privacy rule
docs.text:
• No tool accepts rows about people. run_analysis_on_counts takes only input modes an analysis marks as aggregated.
  • Every result passes through ensure_totals_only before it is returned. If a value from the input, such as a postcode or an area code sent with a count, appears anywhere in a result, the result is withheld.
  • The one exception is a role an analysis marks as reported: a column that holds names the result uses too. For local authorities every value is a public name. For a column that also holds a person's own words, such as their ethnic group, the role lists the exact names the result uses (reported_values, for example "White"), and only those may come back: a charity's own label, such as "Black Caribbean", is still withheld if a result repeats it. Small counts are still hidden, and a value with the shape of a postcode is always withheld.
  • Error messages name the argument that was wrong and never quote its value.
  • The log follows the same rule. When a data source cannot be reached, the log holds the kind of error and not the web address. The code that asks the boundary service logs the address it asked, which holds the area codes of the map, so the connector's command replaces each warning or error from that code with one sentence that says a line was left out. A program that builds the server itself and lets it fetch outlines calls uk_open_data.connector.maps.keep_addresses_out_of_the_log() once to do the same. When a tool crashes, the assistant is told only that the tool failed, and the log says which tool stopped, with what kind of error and where in the code, and leaves out the error's own text, which can quote a value from the rows.
  • An answer given through run_analysis_on_counts is counted with one line on the uk_open_data.runs logger, written by record_run: run analysis=need-reach mode=area_counts door=chat. It holds the analysis, the input mode and the word "chat", each from a fixed list, and nothing from the rows or the options. A run that was held back, refused or withheld is not counted. Nothing is sent anywhere: on your own machine the line goes to stderr with the rest of the log, at any --log-level, and a host counts the lines in the logs it keeps.
  • tests/test_connector_privacy.py calls every tool the way an assistant does and fails if a row-level value reaches a result. A new tool must add a case there.
